about: Every source of the red cabbage pH lab's record (docs/research/cabbage/cabbage.json) and of its primer (src/chem-data/cabbage/primer.ts) that is not a safety data sheet under a bottle's hazards: those are in hazard-manifest.json. Each was fetched and read for this lab on the retrieval date. No source has a copy in this folder. `fetchedSha256` is the sha256 of the file as it was fetched: a record of which file was read, not the hash of anything here, and nothing checks it. Each `supports` row names in `fields` the stored values it supports, gives in `prints` what the source prints, and says in `where` where that is; the build holds the record to these rows. A row whose field is `primer` supports a paragraph of the primer.

sources.citation: Flinn Scientific, Inc. Red Cabbage Indicator: Natural Indicators and Household Substances; Publication No. 91633, three pages, 2016. Read as the PDF the supplier serves at the address above; no copy is kept (retrieved 2026-10-11).

supports.prints: Dark Pink Rose Lavender Purple Blue-violet Dark Blue Blue Teal Emerald Greenish-yellow
supports.where: Page 3, Figure 1: a strip of ten swatches with a name over each and a pH under each: the whole numbers from 2 to 10 in order, and then 11–12. The names are given here in the figure's order, left to right; the last is printed on two lines. Which name stands over which pH was read from the places of the words on the page as well as from their order. The record stores the names in lower case. The figure has no swatch below 2 and none above 12.

Page 2, among the tips, the note marked with a star under the table of suggested things: bleach is basic, which is easy to miss because it soon takes the colour out of the indicator. The record stores the word in this project's spelling.

Page 2, the table of suggested household things, in the column of bases, and the starred note under it: the same passage. It gives no reason for the loss of colour and no time for it; the notes give neither.

Page 3, the caption of the strip of swatches, and the paragraph over it, which says that acid gives the dye its red and pink shades, a neutral liquid its blue and violet, and a base green to yellow. The strip gives one swatch and one name for pH 11–12.

Page 3, the paragraph under this heading: the dyes of red cabbage dissolve in water, are called anthocyanins, and change colour with the pH. Page 1 says that food brought into a laboratory is a laboratory chemical and is not tasted, and that a neutral batch of the indicator is a bluish purple. Page 2 has a cup of distilled water for rinsing the stirrer between one thing and the next.

sources.citation: LibreTexts. Indicators in Foods; a page among the Exemplars of the Ancillary Materials; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-11).

supports.where: Table 1, the pH and colour of anthocyanins: the first row gives pH 1 this colour, and the last gives pH 13 yellow. The rows between give 4, 6, 8 and 12 with blue-red, purple, blue and green. The table is for the dyes of this family in general, taken from petunias in its figure, and not for red cabbage alone; the record uses its two ends only, where the supplier’s figure for red cabbage has nothing.
The same table, and the paragraph after it on red cabbage: a raw extract holds a second group of dyes that has no colour in acid and is yellow in base, so that the mixture looks green in base.

The first part of the page: an indicator is a weak acid whose two forms differ in colour, and the red and the blue of these dyes are such a pair. The paragraph on red cabbage says why its extract shows more colours than two.

supports.where: The table of items in the order of the alphabet, the row Vinegar: 2.40 - 3.40. The row under it gives cider vinegar one figure, 3.10, which lies inside the range.
The same row.
The row for the juice of lemons, whose two figures these are.
The same row.
Under the row Apples, the indented row Juice: 3.35 - 4.00. The meter reads to a tenth, so the lowest reading the model gives is 3.4.
The same row.

The heading of the table's second column. The page says before the table that its ranges are approximate and that foods vary with variety, growing and processing. Of the three, lemon juice has the lowest range; that its range is the lowest of the things on the bench is read from this record's own ranges. The note does not say that it reads lowest in a lab: vinegar's range reaches down to 2.40, and a seed can draw the vinegar under the lemon juice.
The table as a whole: everyday foods with the pH of each.

sources.citation: LibreTexts. The pH Scale; a page of the Supplemental Modules for physical and theoretical chemistry; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-11).

supports.where: In the part on the self-ionisation of water: the constant of water is 1.0 × 10−14 at 25 °C, and its pKw is 14.

Under the heading on the pH scale: the scale is logarithmic, so a step of one whole unit changes the hydrogen ion ten times over; its examples are pH 3 against pH 4, ten times, and pH 3 against pH 5, a hundred times.

The same passages, and with them: pH is worked out as minus the logarithm of how much hydrogen ion a litre holds; a liquid at pH 7 is neutral, with as much hydrogen ion as hydroxide ion; below 7 is acidic and above 7 basic.

supports.where: The page's opening definition: a solution whose pH changes little when a small amount of acid or of alkali goes into it. The page says that an acidic buffer has a pH under 7 and an alkaline one a pH over 7.

supports.where: Part B, on the pH sensor: the probe is rinsed with distilled water before it goes into each of the two buffers it is calibrated in. The page gives no reason and no figure for what an unrinsed probe reads: that is the model's own (parameters.unrinsedSharePercent). That an indicator places a thing to about a unit is this lab's rule for an estimate.
The same part: a pH probe is set against buffers of known pH, pH 4.00 and pH 7.00 there, and drifts with time.
